extracted.intended_audience: Patent owners, in-house and outside IP counsel, patent prosecutors and litigators (U.S. practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, avoiding, and responding to obviousness-type double patenting (OTDP) issues in U.S. patent families, and for using or avoiding terminal disclaimers and other prosecution/litigation strategies in view of patent term adjustment/extension rules. Focuses on portfolio review, prosecution practice, reexamination strategy, and remedial options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type double patenting trigger conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness-type double patenting (nonstatutory double patenting) can be triggered when two patents or applications share patentably-indistinct claims and are commonly-owned, share at least one common inventor or are subject to a joint research agreement (JRA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine is grounded in public policy to prevent unjust extension of the patent 'right to exclude' and harassment from multiple parties asserting essentially the same invention. A determination depends on an assessment of obviousness: if the Subject Patent's claims are not identical but are anticipated by or obvious over the claims of a qualifying Reference Patent (which need not be prior art), the challenged claims are invalid unless cured (e.g., by terminal disclaimer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer content requirements (37 CFR § 1.321(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome an OTDP rejection or finding by filing a terminal disclaimer, the terminal disclaimer must disclaim the terminal portion of the Subject Patent's term that extends past the Reference Patent's full statutory term, including any claims not rejected for OTDP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terminal disclaimer must also include a provision that the Subject Patent shall be unenforceable if it ceases to be commonly owned or, in JRA situations with different owners, commonly enforced with the Reference Patent. See 37 CFR § 1.321(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing requirement for filing terminal disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer must be filed prior to expiration of the relevant Reference Patent(s) to cure OTDP rejections in reexamination or prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Reference Patent has already expired (as in Cellect where all Reference Patents had expired), the option to file a terminal disclaimer during reexamination is not available. Although the Federal Circuit has suggested a terminal disclaimer can sometimes be filed after an adverse OTDP finding (Perricone; Boehringer), it has not ruled that such a filing would operate retroactively to permit damages to accrue before the filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of patent term adjustment (PTA) on OTDP (In re: Cellect ruling)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a patent that has received patent term adjustment (PTA), OTDP must be based on the expiration date of the patent after PTA has been added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim in a patent having a later expiration date solely because of PTA can be invalidated for OTDP over an earlier-expiring patent in the same family. A terminal disclaimer to overcome OTDP must disclaim any PTA beyond an earlier-expiring Reference Patent's expiration date, including any PTA granted to the Reference Patent. The Federal Circuit rejected treating PTA like patent term extension for OTDP purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment difference between patent term extension (PTE) and PTA for OTDP
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent term extension under 35 U.S.C. § 156 (e.g., to compensate for regulatory review delays) and patent term adjustment under 35 U.S.C. § 154 are treated differently in OTDP analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merck and Novartis established that for PTE the OTDP comparison should be made from the expiration date before addition of PTE, and PTE extends beyond a terminal-disclaimer-mandated expiration date. Cellect clarifies that PTA is applied to the expiration date for OTDP, not treated like PTE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of a successful OTDP challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: If a challenged claim is invalidated by OTDP, the entire term of that claim is invalidated, not just the portion that extends past the Reference Patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidation of the full claim term precludes obtaining any infringement remedies, past or present, for OTDP-invalidated claims. This differs from a terminal disclaimer which leaves claims in force but shortens the patent term for all claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff when using a terminal disclaimer vs. other options
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer shortens the patent term for all claims in the Subject Patent, not just those with OTDP problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a terminal disclaimer limits term across the claim set, one should carefully consider whether filing it is worth shortening all claims; alternatives include canceling or amending only the OTDP-invalid claims, statutorily disclaiming claims under 35 U.S.C. § 253(a) (which does not require disclaiming the terminal portion of a granted patent), or arguing patentability with secondary considerations evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio review timing best practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Review patent-family claims sufficiently in advance (e.g., six months) of the expiration of the first-to-expire family member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive review allows filing terminal disclaimers while Reference Patents are still in force or otherwise taking action (cancellation/amendment, statutory disclaimer, prosecution) to avoid running into the situation Cellect faced where Reference Patents had already expired and terminal disclaimers were unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination SNQ and OTDP — prosecution record considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: OTDP may be considered a substantial new question (SNQ) of patentability that justifies granting an ex parte reexamination even if OTDP was not raised during original prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner's mere knowledge of related patents/applications (e.g., via an information disclosure statement) may not show that OTDP was considered during original examination. Patent owners should consider actively requesting on the USPTO record that OTDP over potential Reference Patents be considered, or preemptively filing terminal disclaimers if an OTDP challenge is likely (for example, where an application is a continuation with similar claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using divisional/35 U.S.C. § 121 safe harbor to avoid OTDP
rubrics_metrics.description: An OTDP rejection in a child over a parent can be avoided when the child is considered a divisional application or patent of the parent under 35 U.S.C. § 121.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may try to provoke a restriction requirement in the parent so that a child filed during pendency in response to the restriction requirement qualifies for the § 121 safe harbor (claims directed to subject matter restricted out). Filing multiple patentably-indistinct independent claims (though potentially expensive due to excess claim fees) may help create the circumstances to rely on § 121.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution and litigation tactical recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: If OTDP issues arise, consider alternatives to terminal disclaimers, proactive prosecution steps, and tactics during reexamination or litigation to minimize problems and maximize coverage and patent term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include: (1) preemptively reviewing families and filing terminal disclaimers while possible, (2) considering cancellation/amendment or statutory disclaimer under § 253(a) where appropriate, (3) preserving arguments on patentability (including secondary considerations), (4) actively putting OTDP issues on the USPTO record to avoid SNQ surprises in reexamination, and (5) evaluating whether a Reference Patent still provides sufficient coverage such that filing a disclaimer is unnecessary.
